source.title: On Diversified Preferences of Large Language Model Alignment
source.authors: Dun Zeng; Yong Dai; Pengyu Cheng; Longyue Wang; Tianhao Hu; Wanshun Chen; Nan Du; Zenglin Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out reward-model preference accuracy across different base-model sizes. This is a different measure and setting from held-out pretraining loss, but it bears on the claim version about downstream performance and scale.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or study compute-optimal allocation or architecture shape. It reports reward-model accuracy by test domain and model size; only those accuracy results are recorded as bearing on V6. ECE, reward differences, and the induced Alpaca reject-sampling alignment results are related findings but do not measure V6 as stated.
record.test_reason: Weak T3. Appendix Table 2 reports held-out reward-model preference accuracy for fine-tuned RMs on four base models (Pythia-1.4B, Pythia-2.8B, LLaMa2-7B, LLaMa2-13B), and the authors comment on how it changes with base-model size. This is a fine-tuned downstream task in a new setting, so it bears on V6. However, size is confounded with model family (Pythia vs LLaMa2), no scaling curve is fitted, and nothing is predicted from pretraining loss. The 'scaling law' in the abstract is never fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right; correction. The authors conclude that the impact of diverse preferences depends on model and data size: larger RMs mitigate it and RM accuracy is 'typically proportional to the size of base models'. They also note 13B is not significantly better than 7B. Their main conclusions are that ECE correlates with alignment performance and that MORE improves calibration, especially on shared Helpful/Harmless preferences. They fit no scaling law despite the abstract's wording.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains reward models on diverse preference datasets and compares held-out preference accuracy and calibration across base-model sizes; it does not use the original scaling-law loss measurement or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported reward accuracy varies by preference test dataset and by training scheme. The authors also state that LLaMa2-13B reward accuracy is not significantly better than LLaMa2-7B on their datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: RM calibration error (ECE) varies with base-model size and training scheme. MORE lowers ECE vs MultiTask, and the MultiTask–MORE ECE gap narrows at 13B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-model calibration on mixed preference data depends on base-model size and training scheme.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower RM ECE is associated with better reject-sampling alignment of Alpaca-7B (GPT-4 win rate), when RM accuracy is similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RM calibration predicts RJS alignment quality beyond RM accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The gap between MultiTask accuracy and the single-dataset Top accuracy shrinks with base-model size; at 7B, MultiTask exceeds Top on Oasst1, Webgpt and Summarize.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger RMs absorb diverse, conflicting preference data with less accuracy loss.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the accuracy results. The experiments evaluate reward models on selected preference datasets and do not test extrapolation, predictive fits, or pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: The raw-model and reward-averaging accuracy entries in Appendix C, Table 2 are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit; the selected Top, MultiTask, and MORE entries cover the model-size comparisons and test-dataset variation. ECE and reward-difference results are not rows for V6 because they do not measure downstream-task performance.

untested.parts: All; no pretraining loss is measured.
All; no fits and no extrapolation.
All; no power-law form is fitted for reward modelling.
Predictability: no fitted curve, no prediction from pretraining loss, and no general downstream benchmarks. Only four sizes, split across two model families.

missing.what: Average accuracy across test sets per size and method, e.g. MultiTask 62.38/64.00/70.13/70.90 for 1.4B/2.8B/7B/13B. This is the cleanest size trend.

record.verdict_notes: Size is confounded with model family: Pythia (1.4B, 2.8B) vs LLaMa2 (7B, 13B), with different pretraining data and tokens. Only four points, no uncertainty, and one epoch of fine-tuning. Top is an oracle per-sample ensemble of single-dataset RMs, not a single model. The MORE rows are the study's own method, but are used here only for the within-method size trend. The case for 'tests' is weak; a reviewer could reasonably treat the study as discusses or uses_without_test.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting on small runs and predicting substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The paper measures held-out reward-model preference accuracy, not general downstream-task performance or prediction from pretraining loss; it does not fit or validate a predictive scaling relationship.
Dependence of power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices or setup.

relationships.condition: Pythia-2.8B to LLaMa2-7B RMs, all methods and test sets
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises 2 to 11 points on nearly all test sets (e.g. MT-S 58.95% to 69.30%). Family is confounded with size. Rows T2-L7-*.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased by 2–11 points on nearly all test sets, including MT-S from 58.95% to 69.30%, with family confounded with size.

relationships.reason: Gains are small and inconsistent; Top-Oasst1, Top-Webgpt, MT-Webgpt and MORE-Summ fall (rows T2-P28-TOP-O, -TOP-W, -MT-W, -MORE-S).
relationships.display_finding: Doubling Pythia produced small, inconsistent gains, with Top-Oasst1, Top-Webgpt, MT-Webgpt, and MORE-Summ declining.

relationships.reason: Authors say 13B is not significantly better and attribute this to the datasets being fittable at 7B. MORE drops on three test sets (T2-L13-MORE-O/W/S); others are flat.
relationships.display_finding: LLaMa2-13B was not significantly better than 7B, which the authors attributed to 7B already fitting the datasets; MORE declined on three test sets and other results stayed flat.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reward-model preference accuracy across the five reported test datasets and the Top, MultiTask, and MORE settings
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy is generally higher for larger base models, but several domain/method sequences dip or plateau, and the study does not fit or validate a predictive scaling curve; see the linked rows.
